steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Hitler outlined his foreign policy aims in Mein Kampf (1925) and in a secret meeting with his generals on 5 November 1937 (the Hossbach Memorandum). His three main aims were: to destroy the Treaty of Versailles, to create a Greater Germany by uniting all German-speaking peoples, and to conquer Lebensraum (living space) in eastern Europe.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: In March 1935, Hitler publicly announced German rearmament, directly violating the Treaty of Versailles. He introduced conscription, expanding the army from 100,000 to 550,000 men, and revealed the existence of the Luftwaffe (air force). Britain and France protested but took no action.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: On 13 January 1935, the people of the Saar voted in a plebiscite on their future. Under the Treaty of Versailles, the Saar had been governed by the League of Nations for 15 years. The result was 90.5% in favour of returning to Germany. Hitler celebrated this as a triumph of national self-determination.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: On 7 March 1936, Hitler sent 22,000 German troops into the Rhineland, directly violating the Treaty of Versailles and the Locarno Pact. He later admitted: "The 48 hours after the march into the Rhineland were the most nerve-racking in my life. If the French had marched, we would have had to withdraw." France did not act.

steps.body: Explain why Hitler was able to remilitarise the Rhineland in 1936. (4 marks) | How important was the policy of appeasement in allowing Hitler to achieve his foreign policy aims? (8 marks) | "The Munich Agreement was a mistake." How far do you agree? (12 marks)

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Know the chronological sequence: Saar (Jan 1935) → Rearmament (Mar 1935) → Rhineland (Mar 1936) → Anschluss (Mar 1938) → Sudetenland (Sep 1938) → Czechoslovakia (Mar 1939) Hitler's quote about the Rhineland ("the 48 hours were the most nerve-racking in my life") is excellent evidence that he would have backed down if challenged Always explain WHY Britain and France did not act at each stage - their inaction is as important as Hitler's action The Anglo-German Naval Agreement (June 1935) shows Britain accepted German rearmament Chamberlain's "peace for our time" quote is essential for the Munich Agreement The Czech takeover (March 1939) is the turning point when appeasement was abandoned For "why was Hitler successful" questions, combine Hitler's tactics with the failures of his opponents
